exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function From a Graph

question.text: The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y=f^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2, 5)$ and lies on $y=f.$ The point $B$ has coordinates $(5,2)$ and lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ If $f'(2)=4,$ what is $(f^{-1})'(5)?$
question.explanation:
Since $B \,(5,2)$ lies on $f^{-1},$ we have $f^{-1}(5) = 2.$ We're also told that $f'(2) = 4.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is \[ (f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}. \]

Evaluating at $x=5,$ we have \begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ (f^{-1})'(5) & = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(5))} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{f'(2)} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{4}. } \end{eqnarray}

question.text: The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y=f^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2, 1)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ The point $B$ has coordinates $(1, 2)$ and lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ If $f'(2)=\dfrac{1}{\ln{4}},$ what is $(f^{-1})'(1)? $
question.explanation:
Since $B \,(1,2)$ lies on $f^{-1},$ we have $f^{-1}(1) = 2.$ We're also told that $f'(2) = \dfrac{1}{\ln{4}}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is \[ (f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}. \]

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we have \begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ (f^{-1})'(1) & = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(1))} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{f'(2)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{\ln{4}}\right)} \\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\ln{4}}. } \end{eqnarray}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function

question.text: Consider the function $f(x) = \dfrac{5}{8}\sqrt x$ and the point $P\left(4, \dfrac{5}{4}\right)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at the point $\left(\dfrac{5}{4}, 4\right).$
question.explanation:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $\left(4, \dfrac{5}{4}\right).$ \begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ f(x) &= \dfrac{5}{8}\sqrt x\\[5pt] f'(x) &= \dfrac{5}{16\sqrt x}\\[5pt] f'(4) &= \dfrac{5}{32} } \end{eqnarray}

Since $\left(4, \dfrac{5}{4}\right)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $\left(\dfrac{5}{4}, 4\right)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ (f^{-1})'\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right) &=\dfrac{1}{f'\left(f^{-1}\left(\dfrac {5}{4}\right) \right)} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{f'(4)} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{5}{32}\right)}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{32}{5}. } \end{eqnarray}

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function

question.text: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}x^2+4x+10$ and the point $P(0, 10)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(10, 0).$
question.explanation:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,10).$

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ f(x) &= \dfrac{1}{3}x^2+4x+10\\[5pt] f'(x) &= \dfrac{2}{3}x+4\\[5pt] f'(0) &= 4 } \end{eqnarray}

Since $(0,10)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(10,0)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ (f^{-1})'(10) &=\dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(10))} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{f'(0)} \\ & = \dfrac {1} {4}. } \end{eqnarray}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function Using a Table

question.text:
Find $\left(g\cdot f^{-1}\right)'(3)$ of the product of functions, given the following table of values of $f(x), f'(x),g(x),$ and $g'(x)$ at some points.

$x$ $f(x)$ $f'(x)$ $g(x)$ $g'(x)$
$3$ $-1$ $2$ $4$ $0$
$-2$ $3$ $4$ $1$ $-1$
question.explanation:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$ is \[ (f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}. \]

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function $g(x)f^{-1}(x)$ is \[ (g \cdot f^{-1})'(x)=g'(x)f^{-1}(x) + \dfrac{g(x)}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}. \]

Substituting $x=3,$ we have \[ (g\cdot f^{-1})'(3) =g'(3)f^{-1}(3) + \dfrac{g(3)}{f'(f^{-1}(3))}. \]

From the table, we obtain $f^{-1}(3)=-2,$ $g(3)=4,$ $g'(3)=0,$ and $f'(-2)=4.$ Therefore,

\begin{align*} (g\cdot f^{-1})'(3) &= g'(3)f^{-1}(3) + \dfrac{g(3)}{f'(f^{-1}(3))} \\[5pt] & = 0\cdot (-2) + \dfrac{4}{f'(-2)} \\[5pt] & = 0 + \dfrac{4}{4} \\[5pt] & = 0 + 1\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function Using a Table

question.text:
The following table gives the values of $f(x), f'(x),g(x),$ and $g'(x)$ at some points. Find $(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(5)$ of the product of functions.

$x$ $f(x)$ $f'(x)$ $g(x)$ $g'(x)$
$5$ $-2$ $3$ $-4$ $1$
$-1$ $5$ $-5$ $3$ $-2$
question.explanation:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$ is \[ (f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}. \]

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function $f^{-1}(x)g(x)$ is \[ (f^{-1}\cdot g)'(x)=\dfrac{g(x)}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}+g'(x)f^{-1}(x). \]

Substituting $x=5,$ we have \[ (f^{-1}\cdot g)'(5) =\dfrac{g(5)}{f'(f^{-1}(5))}+g'(5)f^{-1}(5). \]

From the table, we obtain $f^{-1}(5)=-1,$ $g(5)=-4,$ $g'(5)=1,$ and $f'(-1)=-5.$ Therefore,

\begin{align*} (f^{-1}\cdot g)'(5) &=\dfrac{g(5)}{f'(f^{-1}(5))}+g'(5)f^{-1}(5) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{-4}{f'(-1)}+1\cdot (-1) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{-4}{-5}-1 \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{5}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions

question.text: Consider the function $f(x) =x^3+5x+2.$ Given that $y = f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $(f^{-1})'(2).$
question.explanation:
To determine $(f^{-1})'(2),$ we use the following formula: \[ \left(f^{-1}\right)'(2) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(2))} \]

First, we calculate the value of $f^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation $f^{-1}(2) = x.$ This gives \begin{align} f^{-1}(2) & = x\\[3pt] f(x) & = 2\\[3pt] x^3+5x+2 & = 2\\[3pt] x(x^2+5) & = 0\\[3pt] x&=0. \end{align}

Therefore, $f^{-1}(2) =0.$

Now, we calculate $f'(0),$ as follows: \begin{align} f(x) & = x^3+5x+2\\[5pt] f'(x) &= 3x^2+5\\[5pt] f'(0) &= 3\cdot 0+5\\[5pt] f'(0) & = 5 \end{align}

Finally, we get \begin{align} \left(f^{-1}\right)'(2) & = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(2))}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{f'(0)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{5}. \end{align}

example.title: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions

question.text: Consider the function $f(x) = 3x+\sqrt{x}.$ Given that $y = f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $(f^{-1})'(2).$
question.explanation:
To determine $(f^{-1})'(2),$ we use the following formula: \[ \left(f^{-1}\right)'(2) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(2))} \]

First, we calculate the value of $f^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation $f^{-1}(2) = x.$ This gives \begin{align} f^{-1}(2) & = x\\[3pt] f(x) & = 2\\[3pt] 3x+\sqrt{x} & = 2\\[3pt] \sqrt{x} & = 2-3x \\[3pt] x & = 4-12x+9x^2\\[3pt] 9x^2-13x+4&=0 \\[3pt] (9x-4)(x-1)&=0 \\[3pt] x&=\dfrac{4}{9},\,1. \end{align}

Checking the solutions, we notice that only $x=\dfrac{4}{9}$ satisfies the equation $3x+\sqrt{x} = 2.$ Therefore, we discard $x = 1$ and conclude that $f^{-1}(2) = \dfrac{4}{9}.$

Now, we calculate $f'\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right),$ as follows: \begin{align} f(x) & =3x+\sqrt{x}\\[5pt] f'(x) &= 3 + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\\[5pt] f'\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right) &= 3 + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)}}\\[5pt] f'\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right) & = 3+\dfrac{3}{4}\\[5pt] f'\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right) & = \dfrac{15}{4} \end{align}

Finally, we get \begin{align} \left(f^{-1}\right)'(1) & = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(1))}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{f'\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{4}{15}. \end{align}
